characters.name: Grogg
characters.personality: A friendly monster who makes relatable mistakes — perfect for Find-the-Error problems

characters.name: Lizzie
characters.personality: A clever lizard who shows efficient methods and strategic shortcuts

characters.name: Professor Owlbert
characters.personality: A wise owl who explains concepts and reveals the WHY behind math

characters.name: Sir Calculate
characters.personality: A knight who presents boss battles and ultimate challenges

levels.name: The Three-Sided Path
levels.storyContext: Sage Multiplico explains that all paths in the mountains have shapes with meaning.

problems.statement: "Welcome, young explorer! This path is made of triangles. Count the sides of this shape. How many sides does a triangle have?"

hints.text: What does "side" mean for a shape? Think about the straight edges.
Count each straight edge of the triangle one by one.
Start at one corner and trace around — how many edges do you pass?

problems.solutionExplanation: 3 — a triangle has exactly 3 straight sides, one connecting each pair of corners.
problems.teachingPoint: A triangle always has exactly 3 sides and 3 vertices.

levels.name: Classifying Triangles
levels.storyContext: The mountain wall displays three triangles carved by ancient mathematicians.

problems.statement: "Look at these three triangles on the mountain wall. Which one has all sides the same length?" Triangle A: sides 5, 5, 5 Triangle B: sides 5, 5, 3 Triangle C: sides 3, 4, 5

hints.text: What does "all sides the same length" mean mathematically?
Compare the three numbers listed for each triangle — which set has all identical values?
Check Triangle A: are 5, 5, and 5 all the same number?

problems.solutionExplanation: Triangle A (sides 5, 5, 5) — all three sides are equal, making it equilateral.
problems.teachingPoint: Equilateral means all sides equal, isosceles means exactly two sides equal, scalene means no sides equal.

levels.name: Triangle Side Challenge
levels.storyContext: A bridge shaped like a triangle stretches across a ravine.

problems.statement: "The mountain bridge has an isosceles triangle shape. Two sides are 9 units and one side is 4 units. What are all the side lengths?"

hints.text: What does "isosceles" mean about the sides?
An isosceles triangle has exactly two sides that are equal in length.
You know two sides are 9 and one is 4 — list all three: the two equal ones and the different one.

problems.teachingPoint: An isosceles triangle has exactly two equal sides — knowing this lets you find all three side lengths from just two values.

levels.name: The Quadrilateral Crossing
levels.storyContext: The path crosses a bridge shaped like a four-sided figure.

problems.statement: "This bridge has 4 sides. What do we call a shape with 4 sides?"

hints.text: The prefix "quad" gives a clue about the number of sides.
"Quad" means 4 in Latin — what shape name uses this prefix?
The word starts with "Quad" and ends with "lateral" (meaning sides).

problems.solutionExplanation: Quadrilateral — "quad" means 4 and "lateral" means sides.
problems.teachingPoint: "Quad" means 4, "lateral" refers to sides.

levels.name: Special Quadrilaterals
levels.storyContext: The mountain path is paved with four-sided stone tiles.

problems.statement: "Match each quadrilateral to its description: A. Square B. Rectangle C. Parallelogram Which one has 4 equal sides AND 4 right angles?"

hints.text: What properties does a square have that other quadrilaterals might not?
A square has TWO special properties: equal sides AND right angles. Which option matches both?
Check option A (Square) — does it have 4 equal sides AND 4 right angles?

problems.solutionExplanation: A (Square) — it is the only quadrilateral with both 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.
problems.teachingPoint: A square is special because it is BOTH a rectangle (4 right angles) and a rhombus (4 equal sides).

problems.statement: "The summit marker is a shape with 5 sides. What is this polygon called?"

hints.text: Polygon names come from Greek number prefixes. What prefix means 5?
"Penta" means 5 in Greek — what shape name starts with "penta"?
The word is "Penta" + "gon" (meaning angles/corners).

problems.solutionExplanation: Pentagon — "penta" means 5, and a pentagon has 5 sides and 5 angles.
problems.teachingPoint: Pentagon (5), Hexagon (6), Heptagon (7), Octagon (8)

levels.name: Count the Sides
levels.storyContext: Summit markers come in many shapes — count their sides to identify them.

problems.statement: "How many sides does a hexagon have? And an octagon?"

hints.text: Like "pentagon" uses "penta" for 5, what prefixes mean 6 and 8?
"Hex" means 6 and "Oct" means 8 — these are Greek number prefixes.
Hexagon = hex (6) + gon. How many sides? Now do the same for octagon.

problems.solutionExplanation: Hexagon = 6 sides, Octagon = 8 sides. The Greek prefixes "hex" and "oct" tell you the count.
problems.teachingPoint: Greek prefixes tell you the number of sides: penta=5, hexa=6, hepta=7, octa=8.

levels.name: Polyomino Puzzle
levels.storyContext: Crystal fragments in the cave are shaped like connected squares.

problems.statement: "A tetromino is made of 4 unit squares. How many unit squares make up a pentomino?"

hints.text: Notice how the name changes with the number: domino (2), tromino (3), tetromino (4)...
The prefix tells you the count. "Pent" means 5 — like pentagon.
If a tetromino has 4 squares and uses "tetra" (4), a pentomino uses "penta" (5), so...

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 — polyomino names use Greek number prefixes: "penta" means 5, so a pentomino has 5 unit squares.
problems.teachingPoint: Polyominoes are named by their number of squares (domino = 2, tromino = 3, tetromino = 4, pentomino = 5).

levels.name: Build the Shape
levels.storyContext: Crystal fragments must be arranged to fill the cave floor.

problems.statement: "Using exactly 5 unit squares connected edge-to-edge, draw a pentomino that fits inside a 3×3 grid. How many different pentominoes can you make?"

correctAnswer.value: There are 12 distinct pentominoes (not counting rotations/reflections as different). Students need to draw any valid pentomino.
correctAnswer.displayValue: There are 12 distinct pentominoes (not counting rotations/reflections as different). Students need to draw any valid pentomino.

hints.text: Start by thinking about what shapes you can make with 5 connected squares.
Try building pentominoes systematically — start with a row of 5, then try L-shapes, T-shapes, etc.
There are more than 10 but fewer than 15. Try drawing all the ones that fit in a 3×3 grid first.

problems.solutionExplanation: There are 12 distinct pentominoes when rotations and reflections are not counted as different shapes.
problems.teachingPoint: There are exactly 12 distinct pentominoes — systematic counting prevents missing any or counting duplicates.

levels.name: Polyomino Tiling Challenge
levels.storyContext: The ancient cave has a rectangular floor made entirely of pentominoes...

problems.statement: "Can you tile a 5×4 rectangle using exactly 4 pentominoes (with no overlaps and no gaps)? How many unit squares does the rectangle have, and does 4 pentominoes provide enough?"

correctAnswer.displayValue: 20 square units, and yes, 4 pentominoes × 5 squares = 20

hints.text: First calculate the area of the rectangle: 5 × 4 = ?
Each pentomino covers exactly 5 unit squares. How many squares do 4 pentominoes cover?
4 × 5 = 20 = 5 × 4. The areas match! So a tiling is possible (and many solutions exist).

problems.solutionExplanation: 20 square units. 4 pentominoes × 5 squares each = 20, which exactly covers the 5×4 = 20 rectangle. Multiple valid tilings exist.
problems.teachingPoint: Area conservation: a tiling is only possible if the total piece area equals the rectangle area. This is necessary but not always sufficient.

levels.name: Counting by 2s
levels.storyContext: The cave crystals glow in a rhythmic pattern as you walk.

problems.statement: "The cave crystals glow every 2 steps. Starting at 2, what are the next 5 numbers you'll see glowing crystals?"

hints.text: Skip-counting means adding the same number over and over.
Start at 2, then add 2 each time: 2, 2+2=?, 4+2=?, ...
Write out: 2, 4, ... now add 2 three more times.

problems.solutionExplanation: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 — each number is 2 more than the previous one (repeated addition of 2).
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting is repeated addition: 2, 2+2, 2+2+2...

levels.name: Counting by 5s
levels.storyContext: Stepping stones mark every 5th pace through the cavern.

problems.statement: "Count by 5s from 5 to 50. Circle all the numbers that end in 0."

hints.text: First list all numbers when counting by 5s from 5 to 50.
The count goes 5, 10, 15, 20... Which of these end in the digit 0?
Look at the ones place of each number. Circle only those where the ones digit is 0.

problems.teachingPoint: When skip-counting by 5, numbers alternate between ending in 5 and ending in 0.

levels.name: Counting by Different Numbers
levels.storyContext: Stalactites drip at regular intervals, each marking a count.

problems.statement: "Skip-count by 4s starting at 4. What is the 7th number in your count?"

hints.text: The 7th number means you add 4 a total of 7 times starting from 0, or count 7 groups of 4.
Write out the sequence: 4, 8, 12, 16, ... Keep going until you reach the 7th number.
You have 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24... what comes next?

problems.solutionExplanation: 28 — the sequence is 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. The 7th number is 7 × 4 = 28.
problems.teachingPoint: The nth number when skip-counting by k is just n × k — skip-counting IS multiplication.

levels.name: The Hundreds Chart
levels.storyContext: The cave wall shows an ancient hundreds chart.

problems.statement: "On the hundreds chart, start at 7. Add 10. Where do you land? Add 10 again. What pattern do you notice?"

value: 7 → 17 → 27. Pattern: The ones digit stays the same
correctAnswer.displayValue: 7 → 17 → 27. Pattern: The ones digit stays the same, the tens digit increases by 1.

hints.text: Adding 10 moves you down one row on the hundreds chart. What stays the same?
Try it: 7, then 7+10=17, then 17+10=27. Look at the ones digit each time.
The ones digit stays at 7 each time. What happens to the tens digit?

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 → 17 → 27. The pattern: the ones digit stays the same (7), the tens digit increases by 1 each time.
problems.teachingPoint: Adding 10 on a hundreds chart moves down one row — the ones digit never changes, only the tens digit increases by 1.

levels.name: Chart Patterns
levels.storyContext: The cave wall displays an ancient hundreds chart carved in stone.

problems.statement: "What do all numbers in this sequence have in common: 3, 13, 23, 33, 43?"

correctAnswer.value: They all have 3 in the ones place.
correctAnswer.displayValue: They all have 3 in the ones place.

hints.text: Look at each number carefully. What digit appears in every number?
Check the ones place: 3, 13, 23, 33, 43. What digit is always there?
Every number ends in 3 — they all share the same ones digit.

problems.solutionExplanation: They all have 3 in the ones place — they form a column on the hundreds chart.
problems.teachingPoint: Numbers in the same column of a hundreds chart always share the same ones digit.

levels.name: Skip-Count Intersection
levels.storyContext: Two rivers of glowing crystals intersect deep in the cave.

problems.statement: "Ben skip-counts by 6s starting at 6. Jen skip-counts by 9s starting at 9. What is the largest two-digit number that Ben and Jen both say?"

hints.text: What numbers appear in BOTH skip-count sequences? These are common multiples.
List multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24... and multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36... Find overlaps.
Common multiples of 6 and 9 are: 18, 36, 54, 72, 90. Which is the largest two-digit number?

problems.solutionExplanation: Multiples of both 6 and 9: 18, 36, 54, 72, 90. The largest two-digit one is 90.
problems.teachingPoint: Common multiples appear in both skip-count sequences — the smallest common multiple of 6 and 9 is 18 (their LCM).

levels.name: Balance Scale Introduction
levels.storyContext: An old balance scale sits at the cave entrance.

problems.statement: "A balance scale has 15 on the left side. What must go on the right side to balance?"

hints.text: What does "balance" mean? Think about what makes a seesaw level.
A balanced scale means both sides weigh the same amount.
If the left side shows 15, what number on the right makes them equal?

problems.solutionExplanation: 15 — a balanced scale means both sides are equal, so the right side must also be 15.
problems.teachingPoint: When a scale balances, both sides are equal.

levels.name: Missing Number Balance
levels.storyContext: The balance scale holds weights on both sides.

problems.statement: "The left side has: 20 + 10. The right side has: 15 + ___. What goes in the blank to balance?"

hints.text: First figure out what the left side totals. Then the right side must match.
Left side: 20 + 10 = 30. So the right side must also equal 30.
Right side is 15 + ___. What plus 15 equals 30?

problems.solutionExplanation: 15 — the left side totals 30 (20+10), so the right side needs 15+15=30 to balance.
problems.teachingPoint: Balance problems are equations in disguise — both sides must be equal, so find the missing value.

levels.name: Multi-Step Balance
levels.storyContext: The ultimate balance challenge guards the cave exit.

problems.statement: "If 3 triangles balance with 12, how many triangles balance with 20?"

hints.text: First find what ONE triangle is worth using the first balance.
If 3 triangles = 12, divide to find one triangle: 12 ÷ 3 = ?
Each triangle equals 4. Now how many 4s make 20?

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 — each triangle weighs 4 (12 ÷ 3 = 4), so 20 ÷ 4 = 5 triangles balance with 20.
problems.teachingPoint: Solving balance problems step-by-step: first find the unit value, then scale to the target.

levels.name: The Missing Number
levels.storyContext: Sir Calculate claims some numbers can NEVER appear in a skip-count...

problems.statement: "If you skip-count by 4 starting at 4 (4, 8, 12, 16...), will you ever land on 30? Prove your answer."

correctAnswer.value: No! Every number in the sequence is a multiple of 4, and 30 is not a multiple of 4 (30 ÷ 4 = 7 R2).
correctAnswer.displayValue: No — 30 is not a multiple of 4.

hints.text: What do all numbers in the sequence 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... have in common?
They are all multiples of 4. Is 30 a multiple of 4?
Check: 30 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 2. Since the remainder is not 0, 30 is NOT a multiple of 4.

problems.solutionExplanation: No! Skip-counting by 4 only produces multiples of 4. Since 30 ÷ 4 = 7 R2 (remainder is not 0), 30 is not a multiple of 4 and will never appear.
problems.teachingPoint: Skip-counting by n only produces multiples of n — a number that is NOT a multiple can never appear in the sequence.

chapters.name: Perimeter & Area Pass

problems.statement: "You walk around a triangular meadow. The sides are 5 m, 7 m, and 8 m. How far did you walk in total?"

hints.text: If you walk ALL the way around the meadow, which edges do you walk along?
You walk along all 3 sides. Add up all the side lengths.

problems.solutionExplanation: 20 m — perimeter is the total distance around: 5 + 7 + 8 = 20 meters.
problems.teachingPoint: Perimeter = sum of all side lengths.

levels.name: Rectangle Perimeter
levels.storyContext: A rectangular cabin sits at the mountain pass.

problems.statement: "A rectangular cabin has length 10 ft and width 6 ft. What is its perimeter?"

hints.text: A rectangle has two pairs of equal sides. Which sides are equal?
Add all four sides: length + width + length + width.
That is 10 + 6 + 10 + 6. What is the total?

problems.solutionExplanation: 32 ft — perimeter = 10 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 32 feet.
problems.teachingPoint: Rectangle perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width, because opposite sides are equal.

levels.name: Isosceles Triangle Perimeter
levels.storyContext: An isosceles bridge spans a deep gorge.

problems.statement: "What is the perimeter of an isosceles triangle with sides of length 9 and 4?"

hints.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. But WHICH two are equal: the 9s or the 4s?
Could it be 4, 4, 9? Check: can two sides of length 4 reach across a gap of 9?
Triangle inequality: two sides must sum to MORE than the third. Does 4 + 4 > 9?

problems.solutionExplanation: 22 — only 9, 9, 4 forms a valid triangle (4+4=8 < 9 fails the triangle inequality), so perimeter = 9+9+4 = 22.
problems.teachingPoint: The triangle inequality (any two sides must sum to more than the third) eliminates impossible triangles — 4+4=8 < 9, so only 9+9+4 works.

levels.name: Find the Missing Side
levels.storyContext: A mysterious square tile has markings around its edge.

problems.statement: "A square has perimeter 36 cm. What is the length of one side?"

hints.text: A square has 4 equal sides. If you know the total perimeter, how do you find one side?
Perimeter = 4 × side length. So side length = perimeter ÷ 4.
Calculate: 36 ÷ 4 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 cm — since a square has 4 equal sides, each side = 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm.
problems.teachingPoint: Working backwards from perimeter: since all 4 sides of a square are equal, divide perimeter by 4 to find the side length.

levels.name: What is Area?
levels.storyContext: The mountain meadow is divided into unit squares.

problems.statement: "Count the unit squares that cover this rectangle: [3 × 4 grid shown]. What is the area?"

hints.text: Area measures how much flat space a shape covers. How do you measure it?
Count each individual unit square inside the rectangle.
You can count row by row: how many squares in each row, times how many rows?

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 square units — the 3×4 grid has 3 rows of 4, so 3 × 4 = 12 unit squares.
problems.teachingPoint: Area counts the number of unit squares that cover a surface — for rectangles, this equals rows × columns.

levels.name: Rectangle Area
levels.storyContext: The cabin floor needs to be measured for new tiles.

problems.statement: "A cabin floor is 7 meters long and 5 meters wide. What is the area of the floor?"

hints.text: Area of a rectangle = length × width. What are the dimensions here?
Multiply the length (7) by the width (5).
Calculate: 7 × 5 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 35 square meters — area = length × width = 7 × 5 = 35 sq m.
problems.teachingPoint: Area of rectangle = length × width

levels.name: Area vs Perimeter
levels.storyContext: Two explorers debate whether perimeter or area matters more for their campsite.

problems.statement: "A rectangle is 6 units by 3 units. Calculate BOTH its perimeter AND its area."

hints.text: Perimeter and area use different formulas. Recall: perimeter adds sides, area multiplies.
Perimeter = 2×6 + 2×3. Area = 6 × 3. Calculate each.
Perimeter = 12 + 6 = 18. Area = 18. Notice anything surprising?

problems.solutionExplanation: Perimeter = 2(6+3) = 18 units. Area = 6×3 = 18 square units. Same number, different units!
problems.teachingPoint: Different measurements can have the same number but different units!

levels.name: Complex Area
levels.storyContext: The great hall is divided into equal meeting rooms.

problems.statement: "A rectangle with width 21 ft and height 16 ft is split into six congruent rectangles arranged in a 2×3 pattern. What is the area of one small rectangle?"

hints.text: If you know the total area and the number of small rectangles, how do you find one?
First find the total area: 21 × 16. Then divide by 6.
Total area = 336 sq ft. Each small rectangle = 336 ÷ 6 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 56 sq ft — total area = 21 × 16 = 336, divided equally into 6 gives 336 ÷ 6 = 56.
problems.teachingPoint: Dividing area equally means dividing the total by the number of pieces — the arrangement does not change the math.

levels.name: Area Puzzle
levels.storyContext: The architect must design the optimal campsite.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has a perimeter of 20 units. The length and width are whole numbers. What dimensions give the LARGEST possible area?"

hints.text: What whole-number pairs of length and width give a perimeter of 20?
If perimeter = 20, then length + width = 10. List all pairs: (1,9), (2,8), (3,7), (4,6), (5,5).
Calculate each area: 1×9=9, 2×8=16, 3×7=21, 4×6=24, 5×5=25. Which is largest?

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 × 5 = 25 square units. Among all rectangles with perimeter 20, the square maximizes area.
problems.teachingPoint: For a fixed perimeter, the shape closest to a square always has the largest area — this is a fundamental optimization principle.

levels.name: Grogg's Perimeter Blunder
levels.storyContext: Grogg measured the fence around a field, but his math is off...

problems.statement: "Grogg says a 5×8 rectangle has perimeter 26 because 5 + 8 + 5 + 8 = 26. Find his error."

correctAnswer.value: The perimeter is actually 26. Grogg is correct! 5+8+5+8 = 26.

hints.text: Check Grogg's addition carefully: 5 + 8 + 5 + 8.
Add step by step: 5+8=13, 13+5=18, 18+8=26. Is that right?
Actually, 5+8+5+8 = 26 IS correct. This is a trick question — sometimes Grogg gets it right!

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg is actually correct! 5+8+5+8 = 26. The perimeter of a 5×8 rectangle is 26 units. Not every claim contains an error!
problems.teachingPoint: Critical thinking means checking EVERY claim, including ones that seem wrong — sometimes the work is correct and you must recognize that.

levels.name: The Odd Perimeter Question
levels.storyContext: Sir Calculate poses a deep question about rectangles...

problems.statement: "Can a rectangle with whole-number sides have an odd perimeter? Prove your answer."

correctAnswer.value: No! Perimeter = 2(L+W) is always even because multiplying by 2 always gives an even number.

hints.text: What is the formula for the perimeter of a rectangle?
Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). What happens when you multiply ANY number by 2?
Multiplying by 2 always gives an even result. So 2 × (anything) = even. Can it ever be odd?

problems.solutionExplanation: No! Perimeter = 2(L+W). Since 2 times any whole number is even, the perimeter is always even. An odd perimeter is impossible.
problems.teachingPoint: Impossibility proofs use structure — here, the factor of 2 in the perimeter formula guarantees an even result, no matter what L and W are.

signatureContent: Area as covering with unit squares

levels.name: What is Multiplication?
levels.storyContext: Base camp has rows of tents, each holding climbers.

problems.statement: "There are 4 tents at base camp. Each tent has 3 climbers. How many climbers in total? Write this as both addition and multiplication."

hints.text: You have 4 groups of 3. How would you add 3 four times?
Write it as addition first: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = ?
Now write the same thing as multiplication: how many groups × how many in each group?

problems.solutionExplanation: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12, or 4 × 3 = 12. Multiplication is a shortcut for repeated addition.
problems.teachingPoint: Multiplication is a shortcut for repeated addition.

levels.name: Arrays
levels.storyContext: Supply crates are stacked in neat rows and columns.

problems.statement: "The supply crates are arranged in 5 rows with 6 crates in each row. How many crates total?"

hints.text: An array has rows and columns. Count the rows and columns here.
There are 5 rows with 6 in each. Multiply rows × columns.
Calculate: 5 × 6 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 30 — the 5×6 array has 5 rows of 6, giving 5 × 6 = 30 total crates.
problems.teachingPoint: An array shows multiplication visually. Rows × columns = total.

levels.name: Times Tables Practice
levels.storyContext: The multiplication gong rings with each correct answer.

hints.text: Can you break 7 × 8 into facts you already know?
Calculate 7 × 4 = 28. Then add: 28 + 28 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 56 — using the doubling strategy: 7 × 8 = 7 × 4 × 2 = 28 × 2 = 56.
problems.teachingPoint: Breaking harder facts into known facts (like doubling 7×4) is a key mental math strategy.

levels.name: The Commutative Property
levels.storyContext: Two explorers arrange the same supplies in different patterns.

problems.statement: "Is 6 × 4 the same as 4 × 6? Show why using arrays."

value: both equal 24. A 6×4 array has the same number of squares as a 4×6 array.
correctAnswer.displayValue: Yes, both equal 24. A 6×4 array has the same number of squares as a 4×6 array.

hints.text: Draw a 6×4 array and a 4×6 array. Compare them.
Count the total squares in each array. Are they the same?
A 6×4 array can be rotated to become a 4×6 array — same squares, different orientation.

problems.solutionExplanation: Yes, both equal 24. A 6×4 array rotated 90° becomes a 4×6 array — the commutative property says order does not matter.
problems.teachingPoint: a × b = b × a (The Commutative Property)

levels.name: Using Commutativity
levels.storyContext: Lizzie shows a faster way to count the trail markers.

problems.statement: "Which is easier to compute: 8 × 5 or 5 × 8? Explain why and solve."

correctAnswer.value: Both equal 40. Many find 5 × 8 easier because multiplying by 5 follows a simple pattern (ends in 0 or 5).
correctAnswer.displayValue: Both equal 40. Many find 5 × 8 easier because multiplying by 5 follows a simple pattern (ends in 0 or 5).

hints.text: Both expressions give the same answer. But is one easier to compute mentally?
Multiplying by 5 is easy because 5s follow a simple pattern: results end in 0 or 5.
Try 5 × 8: count by 5s eight times, or think of it as half of 10 × 8.

problems.solutionExplanation: Both equal 40. 5 × 8 is often easier because multiplying by 5 gives numbers ending in 0 or 5.
problems.teachingPoint: The commutative property lets you choose the easier order — multiplying by 5 or 10 first is often the smartest move.

levels.name: The Associative Property
levels.storyContext: Three teams of climbers can be grouped different ways.

problems.statement: "Calculate (2 × 3) × 4 and 2 × (3 × 4). What do you notice?"

hints.text: Calculate each expression step by step. Do you get the same answer?
Both equal 24. This works for ANY three numbers — that is the associative property.

problems.solutionExplanation: Both equal 24. (2×3)×4 = 6×4 = 24 and 2×(3×4) = 2×12 = 24. Grouping does not change the product.
problems.teachingPoint: (a × b) × c = a × (b × c) (The Associative Property)

levels.name: Strategic Grouping
levels.storyContext: The supply master groups items for the easiest count.

problems.statement: "Calculate 5 × 7 × 2 by grouping the easy numbers first."

hints.text: Look for two numbers that multiply to give a "friendly" number like 10.
Which two of 5, 7, 2 multiply to make 10?

problems.solutionExplanation: 70 — group 5 × 2 first to get 10, then 10 × 7 = 70. Strategic grouping makes it easy!
problems.teachingPoint: Strategic grouping (associative property) lets you create friendly numbers like 10 or 100 to simplify multiplication.

levels.name: Multiplication Puzzles
levels.storyContext: Ancient puzzles guard the multiplication temple.

problems.statement: "Fill in the blanks: ___ × ___ = 36, where both numbers are greater than 1 and less than 10. Find ALL solutions."

hints.text: Think about which pairs of numbers from 2-9 multiply to give 36.
Start with small factors: does 2 × ? = 36? Does 3 × ? = 36? Continue...
Check: 4 × 9 = 36 ✓. Is there a perfect square? 6 × 6 = 36 ✓. Don't forget reverse order.

problems.solutionExplanation: 4 × 9, 6 × 6, and 9 × 4. These are all factor pairs of 36 with both numbers between 2 and 9.
problems.teachingPoint: Finding all factor pairs systematically means checking each number from 2 upward — stop when factors start repeating.

levels.name: Three-Number Products
levels.storyContext: Three treasure chests each contain treasure to count.

problems.statement: "What is 5 × 4 × 5?"

hints.text: Look for a strategic grouping that makes this easier.
Can you pair two of the numbers to make a friendly product?

problems.teachingPoint: Three-number products can be computed in any order — find the grouping that creates the friendliest intermediate result.

levels.name: Grogg's Multiplication Mistake
levels.storyContext: Grogg proudly shows his work, but something is wrong...

problems.statement: "Grogg says: 6 × 7 = 43 because 6 × 7 = 6 × 6 + 7 = 36 + 7 = 43. Find his mistake and give the correct answer."

hints.text: Grogg tried to break 6 × 7 into 6 × 6 + something. Is that valid?
6 × 7 = 6 × (6 + 1) = 6 × 6 + 6 × 1. Grogg wrote +7 instead of +?
The distributive property says 6 × 7 = 6 × 6 + 6 × 1 = 36 + 6. What is 36 + 6?

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg incorrectly added 7 instead of 6. By the distributive property: 6×7 = 6×(6+1) = 36+6 = 42.
problems.teachingPoint: When breaking apart multiplication, BOTH factors matter: 6 × 7 = 6 × 6 + 6 × 1, NOT 6 × 6 + 7.

levels.name: Quick Comparison
levels.storyContext: Lizzie says sometimes you can compare without calculating exact answers...

problems.statement: "Without multiplying, is 8 × 7 more or less than 50? Explain your reasoning."

hints.text: Can you find a simpler multiplication that you KNOW is at least 50?
You know 8 × 6 = 48 (close to 50). Since 7 > 6, what does that tell you?
8 × 7 > 8 × 6 = 48. But we need > 50. Try: 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 > 7, so 8 × 7 > 49. Still close. Think: 8 × 7 = 56.

problems.solutionExplanation: More than 50. Since 8 × 6 = 48 and 8 × 7 is one more group of 8, we get 48 + 8 = 56 > 50.
problems.teachingPoint: Comparing without calculating uses known benchmarks — you do not need the exact answer to know which side is bigger.

levels.name: What is a Square Number?
levels.storyContext: The Square Tower stands at the mountain peak.

problems.statement: "When you multiply a number by itself, you get a square number. What is 4 × 4?"

hints.text: Multiplying a number by itself gives a special kind of product.
The problem is asking: what is 4 times 4?
Think of 4 groups of 4: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 16 — when you multiply 4 × 4 you get 16, which is called a perfect square (written 4² = 16).
problems.teachingPoint: 16 is a "perfect square" because 4 × 4 = 16. We write this as 4² = 16.

levels.name: Square Arrays
levels.storyContext: Windows in the tower are arranged in perfect squares.

problems.statement: "Draw an array that shows 5 × 5. What shape is it? How many total squares?"

correctAnswer.displayValue: 25 total squares, arranged in a square shape

hints.text: If both dimensions of an array are the same, what shape does the array form?
Draw 5 rows with 5 dots in each. What shape do you see?
Count all the dots: 5 rows × 5 columns = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 25 total squares in a perfect 5×5 square shape — this is why 25 is called a "square number."
problems.teachingPoint: A square number creates a square-shaped array — that is WHY they are called "square" numbers.

levels.name: First Ten Squares
levels.storyContext: Stone tablets list the sacred square numbers.

problems.statement: "Complete this list of perfect squares: 1² = 1, 2² = 4, 3² = 9, 4² = ___, 5² = ___"

hints.text: Each perfect square is a number multiplied by itself.
4² means 4 × 4. What is that? And 5² means 5 × 5.
Calculate: 4 × 4 = ? and 5 × 5 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 4² = 16 and 5² = 25. These extend the pattern: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.
problems.teachingPoint: The first ten perfect squares (1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100) are worth memorizing — they appear everywhere in math.

levels.name: Recognizing Squares
levels.storyContext: You must identify which gemstones are square-shaped.

problems.statement: "Which of these numbers are perfect squares? 20, 25, 30, 36, 40, 49"

hints.text: A perfect square is a number times itself. Check each number.
Test each: is 20 = n×n? Is 25 = 5×5? Is 30 = n×n? Continue for all.
Try finding the square root of each: √25 = 5 ✓, √36 = 6 ✓, √49 = 7 ✓. The others are not whole numbers.

problems.solutionExplanation: 25 (5²), 36 (6²), and 49 (7²) are perfect squares. 20, 30, and 40 are not.
problems.teachingPoint: To test if a number is a perfect square, check whether its square root is a whole number.

levels.name: Square Patterns
levels.storyContext: The ancient mathematician reveals a hidden pattern in perfect squares.

problems.statement: "Look at the differences between consecutive squares: 4-1=3, 9-4=5, 16-9=7, 25-16=9. What's the pattern? What is 36-25?"

correctAnswer.value: 36-25 = 11. Pattern: differences are consecutive odd numbers
correctAnswer.displayValue: 36-25 = 11. Pattern: differences are consecutive odd numbers (3, 5, 7, 9, 11...)

hints.text: Look at the differences: 3, 5, 7, 9. What kind of numbers are these?
They are consecutive odd numbers! What odd number comes after 9?
The next difference is 11. So 36 - 25 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 36 - 25 = 11. The differences between consecutive squares are always consecutive odd numbers: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11...
problems.teachingPoint: The difference between consecutive squares is always an odd number!

levels.name: Building Squares
levels.storyContext: Using the pattern, you can predict the next square number.

problems.statement: "If 7² = 49, use the odd number pattern to find 8²."

hints.text: The pattern says: add the next odd number to get the next square.
Differences so far: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. What comes after 13?
The next odd number is 15. So 8² = 49 + 15 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 8² = 49 + 15 = 64. The next odd number after 13 is 15, continuing the pattern.
problems.teachingPoint: Using the odd-number pattern lets you find the next perfect square from the previous one without multiplying.

levels.name: Area and Squares
levels.storyContext: A garden plot must be measured for planting.

problems.statement: "A square garden has sides of 9 feet. What is the area?"

hints.text: Area of a square = side × side = side².
The side is 9 feet. What is 9 × 9?

problems.solutionExplanation: 81 square feet — area = 9² = 9 × 9 = 81.
problems.teachingPoint: The area of a square with side s is s² — this connects square numbers directly to geometry.

levels.name: Sums of Squares
levels.storyContext: Two square tiles are placed side by side.

problems.statement: "What is 3² + 4²?"

hints.text: Calculate each square separately, then add.
3² = 9 and 4² = 16. Now add them.
What is 9 + 16? Is the result itself a perfect square?

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 + 16 = 25. Remarkably, 25 = 5², so 3² + 4² = 5² — a Pythagorean triple!
problems.teachingPoint: 3² + 4² = 5² is the most famous Pythagorean triple — the sum of two squares can sometimes be another perfect square!

levels.name: Find the Square
levels.storyContext: A secret number times itself opens the vault.

problems.statement: "A number times itself equals 64. What is that number?"

hints.text: You need to find a number that, when multiplied by itself, gives 64.
Try some numbers: 6 × 6 = 36 (too small), 9 × 9 = 81 (too big).
Try 8: what is 8 × 8?

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 — because 8 × 8 = 64. We say √64 = 8.
problems.teachingPoint: Finding a square root means working backwards from the square — what number times itself gives the target?

levels.name: Why Odd Numbers Make Squares
levels.storyContext: Professor Owlbert reveals the deep reason behind the odd number pattern...

problems.statement: "A 3×3 square has 9 dots. To make it a 4×4 square, you add an L-shaped border. How many dots are in the L-shaped border? Why is this always an odd number?"

correctAnswer.value: 7 dots in the L-border (4+4-1=7). It is odd because you add one row (4) + one column (4) minus the shared corner (1) = 2n-1, which is always odd.

hints.text: Draw a 3×3 square. Now extend it to 4×4. What new dots did you add?
You add a new bottom row (4 dots) and a new right column (4 dots), but the corner is shared.
New dots = 4 + 4 - 1 = 7. In general, going from n×n to (n+1)×(n+1) adds 2(n+1) - 1 dots.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 dots in the L-border. You add a row of 4 + column of 4, minus 1 shared corner = 7. Formula: 2n+1 where n is the new side length minus 1.
problems.teachingPoint: The visual L-border proof shows WHY consecutive square differences are odd: adding a row + column - shared corner always gives an odd number.

levels.name: Order of Operations Introduction
levels.storyContext: Two climbers argue about how to evaluate an expression.

problems.statement: "Two climbers solve 3 + 4 × 2 differently. Alex gets 14, Bailey gets 11. Who is correct and why?"

value: Bailey is correct (11). Multiplication comes before addition: 4 × 2 = 8
correctAnswer.displayValue: Bailey is correct (11). Multiplication comes before addition: 4 × 2 = 8, then 3 + 8 = 11.

hints.text: When you have both addition and multiplication, which do you do first?
The rule says: multiplication before addition. So compute 4 × 2 first.

problems.solutionExplanation: Bailey is correct (11). Order of operations: multiply first (4 × 2 = 8), then add (3 + 8 = 11). Alex mistakenly added first.
problems.teachingPoint: Order of Operations: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right). "PEMDAS"

levels.name: Parentheses First
levels.storyContext: The Order of Operations tablet hangs on the temple wall.

problems.statement: "Calculate (3 + 4) × 2"

hints.text: Parentheses override the normal order — do what is inside them first.
First calculate inside the parentheses: 3 + 4 = ?
3 + 4 = 7. Now multiply: 7 × 2 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 14. Parentheses first: (3+4) = 7, then 7 × 2 = 14.
problems.teachingPoint: Parentheses are like saying "do this first!"

levels.name: Practice Order of Operations
levels.storyContext: Professor Owlbert tests your operation ordering skills.

hints.text: Which operation should you perform first in this expression?
Multiplication first: 3 × 4 = 12. Then handle addition and subtraction left to right.
Rewrite as: 20 - 12 + 2. Now go left to right: 20 - 12 = 8, then 8 + 2 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 10. First 3×4 = 12, then left to right: 20 - 12 = 8, then 8 + 2 = 10.
problems.teachingPoint: After handling multiplication, process addition and subtraction left to right — they have equal priority.

levels.name: Area Model Introduction
levels.storyContext: The area model map shows how to break apart multiplications.

problems.statement: "To find 7 × 12, break 12 into 10 + 2. Draw an area model and solve."

hints.text: Breaking a number into parts can make multiplication easier. How would you split 12?
Break 12 into 10 + 2. Then multiply each part by 7 separately.
Draw a rectangle: 7 tall, split into 10 wide and 2 wide. Each part is 7×10 and 7×2.

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 × 12 = 7 × (10+2) = 70 + 14 = 84. The area model shows this as two rectangles that together make the whole.
problems.teachingPoint: The area model visualizes why the distributive property works — splitting a rectangle into parts does not change its total area.

levels.name: The Distributive Property
levels.storyContext: "The ancient Distributive Property lets you 'distribute' multiplication across addition!"

problems.statement: "Use the distributive property to calculate 6 × 15 by breaking 15 into 10 + 5."

hints.text: "Distributing" means multiplying across each part of a sum.
Break 15 into 10 + 5. Then multiply 6 by each part.
Calculate: 6 × 10 = 60 and 6 × 5 = 30. Now add them.

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 × 15 = 6 × (10+5) = 60 + 30 = 90. The distributive property splits a hard multiplication into two easy ones.

problems.statement: "Calculate 8 × 99 using the distributive property."

hints.text: Is there a way to rewrite 99 to make the multiplication easier?
99 is very close to 100. Can you use 100 - 1 instead?

problems.solutionExplanation: 8 × 99 = 8 × (100-1) = 800 - 8 = 792. Breaking 99 into 100-1 makes the calculation easy.
problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property works with subtraction too: a × (b - c) = ab - ac. Using nearby friendly numbers like 100 is a powerful shortcut.

levels.name: Area Model Puzzles
levels.storyContext: A split rectangle on the cave wall hides a multiplication.

problems.statement: "An area model shows a rectangle split into two parts: 5 × 20 and 5 × 3. What single multiplication does this represent?"

hints.text: The area model shows parts of a multiplication. What are the two parts?
5 × 20 = 100 and 5 × 3 = 15. These are parts of what single multiplication?
Since 20 + 3 = 23, the model shows 5 × 23. What is 100 + 15?

problems.teachingPoint: Reading an area model "backwards" means combining the parts — this is how the distributive property connects to visual representations.

levels.name: Complex Expressions
levels.storyContext: The complex expression puzzle guards the temple exit.

hints.text: Follow the order: Parentheses first, then Exponents, then Multiplication, then Addition.
Step 1: (10 - 3) = 7. Step 2: 5² = 25. Now what?

problems.teachingPoint: Complex expressions require disciplined order of operations — work through each step carefully without skipping ahead.

levels.name: Distribution Puzzle
levels.storyContext: Lizzie shows how to "undistribute" for a faster calculation.

problems.statement: "Find the value of 25 × 17 + 25 × 3 without multiplying directly."

hints.text: Both terms share a common factor. What number appears in both 25 × 17 and 25 × 3?
Now calculate: 17 + 3 = 20, and 25 × 20 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 25 × (17+3) = 25 × 20 = 500. Factoring out the common 25 dramatically simplifies the calculation.
problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property in reverse (factoring) turns a hard computation into an easy one by finding common factors.

levels.name: Why Distribution Works
levels.storyContext: Professor Owlbert asks the deep question: WHY does the distributive property work?

problems.statement: "Using an area model, explain WHY 4 × (3 + 5) must equal 4 × 3 + 4 × 5. What makes this true, not just a trick?"

correctAnswer.value: A 4×8 rectangle can be split into a 4×3 and a 4×5 rectangle. The total area does not change — just how you partition it.
correctAnswer.displayValue: Splitting a rectangle does not change its total area.

hints.text: Draw a rectangle that is 4 units tall and (3+5)=8 units wide.
Now draw a vertical line splitting it into a 4×3 part and a 4×5 part. Did any area disappear?
The total area is the same whether you measure it as one rectangle (4×8) or two parts (4×3 + 4×5).

problems.solutionExplanation: A 4×8 rectangle has area 32. Splitting it into 4×3 (12) and 4×5 (20) gives 12+20 = 32. Splitting does not change total area — that IS the distributive property.
problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property is not a "trick" — it is a geometric fact: splitting a rectangle into parts does not change its total area.

levels.name: What is a Variable?
levels.storyContext: A mysterious basket of apples sits on the trail.

problems.statement: "There are some apples in a basket. We don't know how many, so we call the number 'n'. If someone adds 5 more apples, how many apples are there now?"

hints.text: A variable (letter) stands in for a number we do not know yet.
If you have n apples and someone adds 5 more, write that as n plus 5.
In math notation, adding 5 to n is written as n + 5.

problems.solutionExplanation: n + 5 — the variable n represents the unknown count, and adding 5 gives the new total.
problems.teachingPoint: A variable is a letter that represents an unknown number.

levels.name: Expressions with Variables
levels.storyContext: Trail markers use letters to represent unknown distances.

problems.statement: "Write an expression: 'A number x, multiplied by 3'"

hints.text: Translating words to math: "a number x" means the variable x.
"Multiplied by 3" means × 3. How do you write x times 3?
In algebra, x multiplied by 3 is written 3x (or x × 3).

problems.solutionExplanation: 3x or x × 3 — "a number x multiplied by 3" translates directly to this algebraic expression.
problems.teachingPoint: In algebra, we write 3x instead of 3 × x — the multiplication sign is implied when a number is next to a variable.

levels.name: Evaluating Expressions
levels.storyContext: Professor Owlbert gives you a value to substitute.

problems.statement: "If n = 7, what is n + 12?"

hints.text: Evaluating means substituting the given value for the variable.
Replace n with 7 in the expression n + 12.
Calculate: 7 + 12 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 19 — substitute n = 7 into n + 12 to get 7 + 12 = 19.
problems.teachingPoint: Evaluating an expression means replacing each variable with its given value and then computing.

levels.name: Writing Equations
levels.storyContext: The balance scale returns — now with equations.

problems.statement: "Write an equation: 'A number y plus 8 equals 15'"

hints.text: An equation uses "=" to connect two equal things. Translate each word.
"A number y" = y. "Plus 8" = + 8. "Equals 15" = = 15.
Put it together: y + 8 = 15.

problems.solutionExplanation: y + 8 = 15 — an equation uses = to state that two expressions have the same value.
problems.teachingPoint: An equation uses '=' to show two things are equal.

levels.name: Solving by Guess and Check
levels.storyContext: A locked chest opens when you find the right value.

problems.statement: "What value of x makes this true? x + 6 = 14"

hints.text: You need a number that, when you add 6 to it, gives 14.
Try some numbers: does 6 + 6 = 14? Does 7 + 6 = 14?
Think backwards: 14 - 6 = ? That gives you x.

problems.solutionExplanation: x = 8 — because 8 + 6 = 14. You can find this by subtracting: 14 - 6 = 8.
problems.teachingPoint: Solving an equation means finding the value that makes the equation true — use inverse operations or guess-and-check.

levels.name: Inverse Operations
levels.storyContext: The undo button for math: inverse operations.

problems.statement: "To solve n - 5 = 12, what operation undoes subtraction? Solve for n."

hints.text: Subtraction and addition are inverse (opposite) operations.
If n - 5 = 12, undo the subtraction by adding 5 to both sides.

problems.solutionExplanation: Addition undoes subtraction. n = 12 + 5 = 17. Check: 17 - 5 = 12 ✓.
problems.teachingPoint: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations. So are multiplication and division.

levels.name: Multiplication Equations
levels.storyContext: Triangle weights on the balance scale hide a secret.

hints.text: Three identical triangles total 24. What is one triangle worth?
Write as multiplication: 3 × ▲ = 24. What undoes multiplication?
Divide: 24 ÷ 3 = ?

problems.teachingPoint: Symbols like ▲ work just like variables — they stand for unknown values that you can find using inverse operations.

levels.name: Two-Step Equations
levels.storyContext: A two-step lock requires careful equation solving.

hints.text: A two-step equation requires undoing operations in reverse order.
First undo the +4: 2m + 4 = 20 → 2m = 16. Then undo the ×2.
Divide: m = 16 ÷ 2 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: m = 8 — first subtract 4: 2m = 16, then divide by 2: m = 8. Check: 2(8)+4 = 20 ✓.
problems.teachingPoint: Two-step equations: undo addition/subtraction first, then undo multiplication/division — reverse the order of operations.

levels.name: Equation Word Problem
levels.storyContext: The riddle master thinks of a number and challenges you.

problems.statement: "I think of a number, multiply it by 5, then subtract 3. The result is 22. What was my number?"

hints.text: Work backwards from the result. What operations were applied to the mystery number?
The number was ×5 then -3 to get 22. Undo: add 3 first, then divide by 5.

problems.solutionExplanation: 5 — working backwards: 22 + 3 = 25, then 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Check: 5 × 5 - 3 = 22 ✓.
problems.teachingPoint: Working backwards means reversing each operation in reverse order — a powerful strategy for "I think of a number" problems.

levels.name: What is Division?
levels.storyContext: Hikers must split into equal groups for the trek.

problems.statement: "24 hikers need to split into 4 equal groups. How many hikers in each group?"

hints.text: Division means sharing equally. How would you split 24 into 4 equal groups?
Think: what number times 4 gives 24?
Try: 4 × 6 = 24. So each group has how many?

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 — dividing 24 hikers into 4 equal groups gives 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hikers per group.
problems.teachingPoint: Division answers "How many in each group?" or "How many groups?"

levels.name: Division as Reverse Multiplication
levels.storyContext: The multiplication-division connection is carved on the wall.

hints.text: Division and multiplication are inverse operations — they undo each other.
If 7 × 8 = 56, then 56 ÷ 8 must give back one of the original numbers.
56 ÷ 8 = ? (which factor is missing?)

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 — since 7 × 8 = 56, dividing 56 by 8 gives back 7. Division undoes multiplication.
problems.teachingPoint: Division undoes multiplication. If a × b = c, then c ÷ b = a.

levels.name: Division Facts
levels.storyContext: Quick division facts unlock the next passage.

hints.text: Think: what number times 9 gives 63?
Try the 9 times table: 9×5=45, 9×6=54, 9×7=?

problems.solutionExplanation: 7 — from the multiplication fact 9 × 7 = 63, we get 63 ÷ 9 = 7.
problems.teachingPoint: Division facts are just multiplication facts read backwards — knowing one gives you the other for free.

levels.name: Division with Arrays
levels.storyContext: Dots on the cave ceiling form a perfect array.

problems.statement: "45 dots are arranged in 5 equal rows. How many dots in each row? Write this as a division."

hints.text: An array with 45 dots in 5 equal rows — how many per row?
This is a division problem: 45 ÷ 5 = ?
Think: 5 × ? = 45. Try 5 × 9.

problems.solutionExplanation: 9 dots per row. 45 ÷ 5 = 9. The array shows 5 rows of 9.
problems.teachingPoint: Arrays connect multiplication and division visually — the same array shows both 5 × 9 = 45 and 45 ÷ 5 = 9.

levels.name: What are Remainders?
levels.storyContext: Not everyone fits into a group — some are left over.

problems.statement: "14 hikers want to form groups of 3. How many complete groups? How many hikers are left over?"

hints.text: When you cannot divide evenly, there is a remainder — the "left over" amount.
How many complete groups of 3 can you make from 14?
Try: 3 × 4 = 12 (fits), 3 × 5 = 15 (too big). So 4 groups with 14 - 12 = ? left over.

problems.solutionExplanation: 4 groups with 2 left over (14 ÷ 3 = 4 R2). The remainder is what cannot fill another complete group.
problems.teachingPoint: The leftover is called the "remainder." We write 14 ÷ 3 = 4 R2.

levels.name: Finding Remainders
levels.storyContext: The remainder reveals which path to take.

problems.statement: "What is 23 ÷ 5?"

hints.text: Find the largest multiple of 5 that does not exceed 23.
5 × 4 = 20, 5 × 5 = 25 (too big). So the quotient is 4.
The remainder is 23 - 20 = ?

problems.teachingPoint: To find a remainder: find the largest multiple of the divisor that fits, then subtract it from the dividend.

levels.name: Remainder Patterns
levels.storyContext: A pattern in remainders unlocks the cipher.

problems.statement: "When dividing by 6, what are all the possible remainders?"

hints.text: When dividing by 6, the remainder is what is "left over" after grouping by 6.
Can the remainder ever be 6 or more? Think about what would happen.
If the remainder were 6, you could make another group! So remainders must be less than the divisor.

problems.solutionExplanation: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — the remainder when dividing by 6 is always less than 6.
problems.teachingPoint: The remainder is always less than the divisor — if it were equal or larger, you could make another complete group.

levels.name: Remainder Word Problem
levels.storyContext: The baker at base camp needs help boxing cookies.

problems.statement: "A baker has 50 cookies. She puts 8 cookies in each box. How many full boxes can she make? How many cookies are left over?"

hints.text: How many times does 8 fit into 50 without going over?
Try: 8 × 6 = 48 (fits), 8 × 7 = 56 (too big).
So 6 full boxes. The leftovers: 50 - 48 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 6 full boxes with 2 cookies left over. 50 ÷ 8 = 6 R2 (8×6=48, 50-48=2).
problems.teachingPoint: In real-world division, the remainder matters: you can only count COMPLETE boxes, and the remainder tells you what is left.

levels.name: Chicken McNugget Problem
levels.storyContext: An ancient weight puzzle with special constraints.

problems.statement: "Fubert has only 3-gram and 7-gram weights. What is the largest weight that he CANNOT make by combining two or more of these weights?"

hints.text: List the weights you CAN make using only 3-gram and 7-gram weights.
You can make: 3, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16... Which ones are MISSING?
Cannot make: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 11. What is the largest number in this list?

problems.teachingPoint: This is a Frobenius/coin problem — for two coprime values a and b, the largest impossible value is ab - a - b.

levels.name: Grogg's Remainder Riddle
levels.storyContext: Grogg divided some trail mix, but his remainder seems too big...

problems.statement: "Grogg says 29 ÷ 4 = 6 R5. What went wrong?"

correctAnswer.value: The remainder 5 is bigger than the divisor 4. Correct: 29 ÷ 4 = 7 R1.

hints.text: What is the rule about remainders and divisors?
A remainder must ALWAYS be less than the divisor. Is 5 < 4?
Since 5 ≥ 4, Grogg can make one more group. Try 4 × 7 = 28, remainder = 29 - 28 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg's remainder (5) exceeds the divisor (4), which is impossible. Correct: 4 × 7 = 28, remainder = 29 - 28 = 1. So 29 ÷ 4 = 7 R1.
problems.teachingPoint: A remainder must ALWAYS be less than the divisor — if it is not, you can fit one more group.

levels.name: Units of Length
levels.storyContext: Trail signs use different measurement units.

problems.statement: "How many inches are in 1 foot? How many feet are in 1 yard?"

hints.text: These are standard measurement conversions. Do you remember the relationships?
A ruler is 12 inches long and equals 1 foot. A yard is 3 of those rulers.
Count: 12 inches = 1 foot. And 3 feet laid end to end = 1 yard.

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 inches = 1 foot, 3 feet = 1 yard. These are key measurement facts to memorize.
problems.teachingPoint: Measurement conversions are multiplication/division facts: 12 in = 1 ft, 3 ft = 1 yd, 5280 ft = 1 mi.

levels.name: Converting Units
levels.storyContext: A ruler at the trailhead helps convert measurements.

problems.statement: "Convert 36 inches to feet."

hints.text: To convert smaller units to larger units, you divide.
There are 12 inches in a foot. How many groups of 12 are in 36?
Calculate: 36 ÷ 12 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 3 feet — divide 36 inches by 12 inches per foot: 36 ÷ 12 = 3.
problems.teachingPoint: Converting to larger units means dividing — fewer larger units are needed to represent the same length.

levels.name: Metric Units
levels.storyContext: The metric trail uses centimeters and meters.

problems.statement: "How many centimeters are in 1 meter? How many meters in 1 kilometer?"

hints.text: Metric units are based on powers of 10 — much simpler than customary units.
"Centi" means 100 and "kilo" means 1000.
So 1 meter = 100 centimeters, and 1 kilometer = 1000 meters.

problems.solutionExplanation: 100 cm = 1 m and 1000 m = 1 km. The metric system uses powers of 10.
problems.teachingPoint: Metric prefixes indicate powers of 10: centi = 1/100, kilo = 1000. This makes metric conversions simpler than customary.

levels.name: Metric Conversions
levels.storyContext: A long rope must be measured in the right units.

problems.statement: "Convert 250 centimeters to meters."

hints.text: To convert cm to m, divide by 100 (since 100 cm = 1 m).
Calculate: 250 ÷ 100 = ?
250 ÷ 100 = 2.5. That is 2 meters and 50 centimeters.

problems.solutionExplanation: 2.5 meters (or 2 m 50 cm) — divide 250 by 100 since there are 100 cm per meter.
problems.teachingPoint: Dividing by 100 converts centimeters to meters — just move the decimal point two places left.

levels.name: Weight/Mass Units
levels.storyContext: Climbing gear is weighed before the ascent.

problems.statement: "A climbing rope weighs 2 kilograms. How many grams is that?"

hints.text: "Kilo" means 1000. How does this apply to grams and kilograms?
1 kilogram = 1000 grams. So 2 kilograms = ?
Multiply: 2 × 1000 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 2000 grams — since 1 kg = 1000 g, multiply 2 × 1000 = 2000 g.
problems.teachingPoint: The "kilo" prefix always means 1000 of the base unit: kilogram = 1000 grams, kilometer = 1000 meters.

levels.name: Time Units
levels.storyContext: A long hike requires careful time planning.

problems.statement: "A hike takes 3 hours and 45 minutes. How many minutes total?"

hints.text: To convert hours to minutes, you need to know how many minutes are in one hour.
There are 60 minutes in 1 hour. Multiply hours by 60, then add extra minutes.
Calculate: 3 × 60 = 180. Then add 45: 180 + 45 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 225 minutes — 3 hours = 3 × 60 = 180 minutes, plus 45 = 225 total.
problems.teachingPoint: Time conversion: hours × 60 gives minutes. Always convert the hours first, then add remaining minutes.

levels.name: Coin Problem
levels.storyContext: Coins found in an old pack pose a counting puzzle.

problems.statement: "Max has 7 US coins that are worth a total of 48 cents. How many nickels does he have?"

hints.text: You need 7 US coins totaling 48 cents. Think about which coin types to use.
Start with larger coins. A quarter is 25¢. If you use one quarter, you need 23¢ from 6 coins.
Try: 1 quarter (25¢) + 1 dime (10¢) = 35¢ from 2 coins. Need 13¢ from 5 coins. How?

problems.solutionExplanation: 2 nickels. One solution: 1 quarter + 1 dime + 2 nickels + 3 pennies = 25+10+10+3 = 48¢ with 7 coins.
problems.teachingPoint: Coin problems require systematic trial — start with the largest coins and work down, checking the count constraint.

levels.name: Challenge Review
levels.storyContext: A perimeter-to-area challenge connects two concepts.

problems.statement: "A square has the same perimeter as a rectangle that is 10 units long and 6 units wide. What is the area of the square?"

hints.text: This connects perimeter and area. First find the perimeter of the rectangle.
Rectangle perimeter = 2(10+6) = 32. The square has the same perimeter. What is its side?
Square perimeter = 4 × side = 32. So side = 32 ÷ 4 = 8. Now find area: 8 × 8 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 64 square units. Rectangle perimeter = 2(10+6) = 32. Square side = 32÷4 = 8. Area = 8² = 64.
problems.teachingPoint: A square and rectangle can share the same perimeter but have very different areas — the square always has more.

levels.name: Variable Valley Challenge
levels.storyContext: Variables and remainders combine in the final challenge.

problems.statement: "If n ÷ 7 has a remainder of 3, and n is between 30 and 40, what is n?"

hints.text: You need a number between 30 and 40 that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 7.
Check multiples of 7 near 30-40: 7×4=28, 7×5=35. Add 3 to each.
28 + 3 = 31 ✓ (between 30-40). 35 + 3 = 38 ✓ (between 30-40). Both work!

problems.solutionExplanation: 31 or 38 — both leave remainder 3 when divided by 7 (7×4+3=31, 7×5+3=38).
problems.teachingPoint: Remainder problems have multiple solutions spaced evenly apart — the gap equals the divisor.

levels.name: What is a Fraction?
levels.storyContext: Pizza at base camp introduces the concept of fractions.

problems.statement: "A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. You eat 3 slices. What fraction of the pizza did you eat?"

hints.text: A fraction names part of a whole. What are the two parts of a fraction?
The denominator is the total slices (8). The numerator is how many you ate (3).
Write it as: slices eaten / total slices = 3/?

problems.solutionExplanation: 3/8 — the numerator (3) is the parts you ate, the denominator (8) is the total equal parts.
problems.teachingPoint: A fraction has a numerator (parts you have) and denominator (total equal parts).

levels.name: Unit Fractions
levels.storyContext: Each climber gets one fair share of supplies.

problems.statement: "What is the unit fraction for 'one out of five equal parts'?"

hints.text: A unit fraction means exactly ONE part out of the total.
If there are 5 equal parts and you take 1, the fraction has 1 on top.
The numerator is 1 and the denominator is 5: write as 1/?

problems.solutionExplanation: 1/5 — a unit fraction always has 1 as the numerator, with the denominator showing the total parts.
problems.teachingPoint: Unit fractions have 1 as the numerator: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5...

levels.name: Reading Fractions
levels.storyContext: A shaded rectangle shows a fraction visually.

problems.statement: "A rectangle is divided into 6 equal parts. 4 parts are shaded. What fraction is shaded?"

hints.text: Count the total parts and the shaded parts separately.
Total equal parts = 6 (denominator). Shaded parts = 4 (numerator).
Write the fraction: shaded/total = 4/?

problems.solutionExplanation: 4/6 — there are 6 equal parts total and 4 are shaded.
problems.teachingPoint: Reading a fraction from a picture: count total equal parts (denominator) and shaded parts (numerator).

levels.name: Whole-Number Fractions
levels.storyContext: When you have all the parts, you have a whole.

problems.statement: "What whole number equals 12/4?"

hints.text: When the numerator divides evenly by the denominator, the fraction equals a whole number.
Treat the fraction as a division: 12 ÷ 4 = ?
If you have 12 parts and each whole needs 4 parts, you have 12 ÷ 4 = ? wholes.

problems.solutionExplanation: 3 — because 12 ÷ 4 = 3. When the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, the fraction simplifies to a whole number.
problems.teachingPoint: When the numerator is a multiple of the denominator, the fraction equals a whole number.

levels.name: Fractions Greater Than 1
levels.storyContext: More pizza than one whole? Fractions can be greater than 1.

problems.statement: "You have 7/4 of a pizza. Is this more or less than 1 whole pizza? How much more?"

correctAnswer.displayValue: More than 1. It equals 1 and 3/4 pizzas (or 1¾).

hints.text: Compare the numerator to the denominator. When the numerator is bigger, what does that mean?
7/4 means you have 7 parts, but each whole pizza only has 4 parts.
7 parts = 4 parts (1 whole) + 3 parts (3/4). So it equals 1 and ?/4.

problems.solutionExplanation: More than 1. 7/4 = 1 and 3/4 (or 1¾). Seven quarter-slices is one whole pizza plus three more quarters.
problems.teachingPoint: When the numerator exceeds the denominator, the fraction is greater than 1 — these are called improper fractions.

levels.name: Mixed Numbers
levels.storyContext: Trail rations come in mixed amounts.

problems.statement: "Write 11/3 as a mixed number."

hints.text: A mixed number has a whole part and a fraction part. Divide to find them.
Divide: 11 ÷ 3 = ? with remainder ?
11 ÷ 3 = 3 remainder 2. The whole part is 3, the fraction part is 2/3.

problems.solutionExplanation: 3⅔ — divide 11 by 3: quotient 3, remainder 2. So 11/3 = 3 and 2/3.
problems.teachingPoint: To convert an improper fraction to a mixed number: divide numerator by denominator. Quotient = whole, remainder = new numerator.

levels.name: Fractions on a Number Line
levels.storyContext: A number line on the trail shows where fractions live.

problems.statement: "Place 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1. Is it closer to 0 or to 1?"

hints.text: On a number line from 0 to 1, where does 3/4 fall? Think about how many quarters fit.
1/4 is at the first quarter mark, 2/4 (= 1/2) is at the midpoint, 3/4 is at the third quarter.
Is 3/4 closer to 0 (the start) or 1 (the end)?

problems.solutionExplanation: Closer to 1 — on the number line, 3/4 is three-quarters of the way to 1, well past the halfway point.
problems.teachingPoint: Number lines help visualize fraction size — 3/4 is three-quarters of the way from 0 to 1, clearly closer to 1.

levels.name: Comparing Unit Fractions
levels.storyContext: Which share is bigger? Think before you calculate.

problems.statement: "Which is larger: 1/3 or 1/5? Explain why."

hints.text: With unit fractions, more parts means SMALLER pieces. Why?
Imagine cutting a pizza into 3 slices vs 5 slices. Which slices are bigger?
Fewer cuts = bigger pieces. So 1/3 (fewer cuts) gives bigger pieces than 1/5.

problems.solutionExplanation: 1/3 is larger. With unit fractions, a smaller denominator means bigger pieces — cutting into 3 gives larger slices than cutting into 5.
problems.teachingPoint: With unit fractions, the SMALLER denominator means LARGER pieces!

levels.name: Comparing Fractions
levels.storyContext: Three fractions must be ordered from smallest to largest.

problems.statement: "Put in order from smallest to largest: 2/5, 2/3, 2/7"

hints.text: All three fractions have the same numerator (2). How does the denominator affect size?
Same numerator: larger denominator = smaller pieces = smaller fraction.
Order denominators from largest (smallest fraction) to smallest (largest fraction): 7, 5, 3.

problems.solutionExplanation: 2/7, 2/5, 2/3. Same numerator so: largest denominator (7) = smallest value, smallest denominator (3) = largest value.
problems.teachingPoint: When numerators are equal, fractions with larger denominators are SMALLER — more parts means each part is smaller.

levels.name: Grogg's Fraction Confusion
levels.storyContext: Grogg thinks bigger denominators mean bigger fractions...

problems.statement: "Grogg says 3/8 > 1/2 because 8 > 2. Find his mistake."

correctAnswer.value: Wrong! 1/2 = 4/8, and 3/8 < 4/8. Bigger denominator means SMALLER pieces, not bigger fractions.

hints.text: Grogg compared denominators directly. Is a bigger denominator always better?
Convert to the same denominator: 1/2 = ?/8. Then compare.
1/2 = 4/8. Now compare: is 3/8 bigger or smaller than 4/8?

problems.solutionExplanation: Grogg confused "bigger denominator" with "bigger fraction." In truth, 1/2 = 4/8, and 3/8 < 4/8, so 3/8 < 1/2.
problems.teachingPoint: A larger denominator means MORE pieces, so each piece is SMALLER. You must compare fractions using common denominators or benchmarks.

levels.name: Fraction Quick Compare
levels.storyContext: Lizzie challenges you to compare without converting...

problems.statement: "Without finding common denominators, is 3/8 more or less than 1/2?"

hints.text: Think about what "half" means in terms of eighths.
Half of 8 is 4, so 1/2 = 4/8. Is 3 more or less than 4?
3/8 < 4/8 = 1/2. You only needed to compare 3 to half the denominator.

problems.solutionExplanation: Less than 1/2. Half of 8 is 4, so 1/2 = 4/8. Since 3 < 4, we know 3/8 < 1/2 without any calculation.
problems.teachingPoint: Quick fraction benchmark: compare the numerator to half the denominator. If smaller, the fraction is less than 1/2.

levels.name: What is Estimation?
levels.storyContext: Quick estimates help plan the expedition.

problems.statement: "About how many days are in 3 months? (Don't calculate exactly!)"

hints.text: Estimation means getting a reasonable answer quickly, not an exact one.
About how many days are in one month? Use a round number.
Roughly 30 days per month. So 3 months ≈ 3 × 30 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: About 90 days — using roughly 30 days per month, 3 × 30 = 90. The exact answer (89-92) varies but 90 is an excellent estimate.
problems.teachingPoint: Estimation gives a quick, reasonable answer without exact calculation.

levels.name: Rounding to Nearest 10
levels.storyContext: Rounding simplifies trail distances.

problems.statement: "Round 47 to the nearest 10."

hints.text: To round to the nearest 10, look at the ones digit.
The ones digit of 47 is 7. Is 7 closer to 0 (round down) or 10 (round up)?
7 ≥ 5, so round up. 47 rounds up to 50.

problems.solutionExplanation: 50 — the ones digit is 7 (≥ 5), so 47 rounds up to 50.
problems.teachingPoint: Look at the ones digit. 5 or more rounds up, 4 or less rounds down.

levels.name: Rounding to Nearest 100
levels.storyContext: Mountain heights are rounded to the nearest hundred.

problems.statement: "Round 849 to the nearest hundred."

hints.text: To round to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit.
In 849, the tens digit is 4. Is that 5 or more (round up) or less than 5 (round down)?
4 < 5, so round down. 849 rounds down to 800.

problems.solutionExplanation: 800 — the tens digit is 4 (< 5), so 849 rounds down to 800.
problems.teachingPoint: Rounding to the nearest hundred: look at the tens digit. If 5+, round up; if less, round down.

levels.name: Estimating Sums
levels.storyContext: Adding approximate distances to plan the route.

problems.statement: "Estimate 389 + 512 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred first."

hints.text: Round each number to the nearest hundred first, then add.
389 rounds to 400. 512 rounds to 500.
Now add the rounded values: 400 + 500 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 400 + 500 = 900. The actual answer (901) is very close, showing this estimate is excellent.
problems.teachingPoint: Estimating sums by rounding gives a quick ballpark — useful for checking if exact calculations are reasonable.

levels.name: Estimating Products
levels.storyContext: Estimating large products for supply orders.

problems.statement: "Estimate 29 × 41 by rounding."

hints.text: Round each factor to the nearest 10 to make multiplication easier.
29 rounds to 30. 41 rounds to 40.
Estimate: 30 × 40 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 30 × 40 = 1,200. The actual answer (1,189) is close, confirming the estimate is reasonable.
problems.teachingPoint: Estimating products by rounding factors to the nearest 10 gives quick ballpark answers for multiplication.

levels.name: Estimating Quotients
levels.storyContext: Dividing supplies approximately among hikers.

problems.statement: "Estimate 247 ÷ 5 without dividing exactly."

hints.text: For estimation, round the dividend to a nearby number that divides evenly.
247 is close to 250. Does 250 divide evenly by 5?

problems.solutionExplanation: About 50 — round 247 to 250, then 250 ÷ 5 = 50. The actual answer (49.4) confirms this is a great estimate.
problems.teachingPoint: Round the dividend to a number that divides evenly.

levels.name: Is My Answer Reasonable?
levels.storyContext: A student's calculation seems off — use estimation to check.

problems.statement: "A student calculated 58 × 7 = 486. Is this reasonable? Estimate to check."

correctAnswer.displayValue: Not reasonable. Estimate: 60 × 7 = 420, so 486 is too high.

hints.text: Use estimation to check if the student's answer makes sense.
Round 58 to 60 for easier multiplication. What is 60 × 7?
60 × 7 = 420. The student got 486, which is much higher than 420. Is that reasonable?

problems.solutionExplanation: Not reasonable. Estimate: 60 × 7 = 420, but the student got 486 (too high). The actual answer is 58 × 7 = 406.
problems.teachingPoint: Estimation is a powerful checking tool — if an exact answer is far from a quick estimate, the calculation likely has an error.

levels.name: Fermi Estimation
levels.storyContext: How many minutes until the summit? A Fermi challenge.

problems.statement: "About how many minutes are in one week? (Estimate without a calculator)"

hints.text: Break this into steps: minutes per hour × hours per day × days per week.
Estimate each: 60 min/hr × 24 hr/day × 7 days. Round 24 to 25 for easier math.

problems.solutionExplanation: About 10,000 minutes. Estimate: 60 × 25 × 7 ≈ 10,500. Actual: 60 × 24 × 7 = 10,080.
problems.teachingPoint: Fermi estimation breaks big questions into smaller, estimable pieces — a key real-world math skill.

levels.name: Strategic Estimation
levels.storyContext: Budget estimation: can you afford enough books for the team?

problems.statement: "You have $100. Books cost $13 each. Estimate: can you buy 8 books?"

hints.text: You need to know if 8 books at $13 each costs more or less than $100.
Round $13 up to make the estimate clearer. What is $15 × 8?
$15 × 8 = $120 > $100. Since $13 < $15, the actual cost is between $104 and $120. Either way, over budget.

problems.solutionExplanation: No. $13 × 8 = $104 > $100. Estimating: $15 × 8 = $120 makes it even clearer the budget is exceeded.
problems.teachingPoint: Strategic estimation means choosing whether to round up or down based on what question you are answering — here, rounding UP proves it exceeds $100.

chapters.name: Area Measurement Mastery

levels.name: Area Units
levels.storyContext: Why are area units "squared"? The answer lies in geometry.

problems.statement: "Why do we measure area in 'square feet' or 'square meters' instead of just 'feet' or 'meters'?"

correctAnswer.displayValue: Because area measures 2-dimensional space (length × width), which gives square units.

hints.text: Length measures one dimension (a line). Area measures how much surface a shape covers.
When you multiply length × width, the units also multiply: feet × feet = ?
Just as 3 × 4 = 12, feet × feet = square feet. Two dimensions give "square" units.

problems.solutionExplanation: Area measures 2-dimensional space (length × width). Multiplying two length units gives square units (ft × ft = sq ft).
problems.teachingPoint: Area uses square units because it measures 2D space — multiplying two lengths gives a squared unit.

levels.name: Area of Rectangles Review
levels.storyContext: The base camp rectangle needs tiling.

problems.statement: "Find the area of a rectangle with length 15 cm and width 8 cm."

hints.text: Area of a rectangle = length × width.
Multiply: 15 × 8. Break it up: 15 × 8 = (10 × 8) + (5 × 8).

problems.solutionExplanation: 120 square centimeters — area = 15 × 8 = 120. Using distributive: (10×8) + (5×8) = 80 + 40 = 120.
problems.teachingPoint: The distributive property makes large area calculations manageable: break one dimension into friendly parts.

levels.name: Area of Squares Review
levels.storyContext: A square garden plot at the summit.

problems.statement: "A square garden has sides of 12 meters. What is its area?"

hints.text: A square has equal sides, so area = side × side = side².
The side is 12 meters. What is 12 × 12?

problems.solutionExplanation: 144 square meters — area = 12² = 12 × 12 = 144.
problems.teachingPoint: Square area connects directly to perfect squares — a 12m square has area 12² = 144.

levels.name: Triangle Area Introduction
levels.storyContext: A diagonal cut creates something new.

problems.statement: "A rectangle has area 24 square units. A triangle is made by cutting the rectangle diagonally in half. What is the triangle's area?"

hints.text: A diagonal cut splits a rectangle into two equal triangles.
If the whole rectangle has area 24, what is half of it?

problems.solutionExplanation: 12 square units — cutting a rectangle diagonally gives two equal triangles, each with half the rectangle's area.
problems.teachingPoint: Triangle area = ½ × base × height

levels.name: Triangle Area Formula
levels.storyContext: A triangular sail needs measuring.

problems.statement: "Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm."

hints.text: Triangle area = ½ × base × height.
Plug in: ½ × 10 × 6. Calculate step by step.
First: 10 × 6 = 60. Then half: 60 ÷ 2 = ?

problems.teachingPoint: Triangle area = ½ × base × height. The ½ comes from the triangle being half of a rectangle with the same base and height.

levels.name: Finding Base or Height
levels.storyContext: The height of a triangle is hidden — find it from the area.

problems.statement: "A triangle has area 35 square units and base 7 units. What is the height?"

hints.text: You know the area formula and two of three values. Solve for the missing one.
Area = ½ × base × height. Plug in: 35 = ½ × 7 × h.
Simplify: 35 = 3.5 × h. Divide both sides by 3.5: h = 35 ÷ 3.5 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 10 units — from 35 = ½ × 7 × h, get 35 = 3.5h, so h = 10.
problems.teachingPoint: Working backwards from area: if you know area and one dimension, use inverse operations to find the missing dimension.

levels.name: Composite Shapes
levels.storyContext: An L-shaped cabin has two rectangular rooms.

problems.statement: "An L-shaped figure is made of two rectangles: one is 5×3 and the other is 4×2. What is the total area?"

hints.text: Composite shapes can be broken into simpler shapes you know how to measure.
Find the area of each rectangle separately, then add.
Rectangle 1: 5 × 3 = 15. Rectangle 2: 4 × 2 = 8. Total = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 15 + 8 = 23 square units. Break the L-shape into two rectangles and add their areas.
problems.teachingPoint: Composite area = sum of parts. Break complex shapes into rectangles and triangles you can measure individually.

levels.name: Subtracting Areas
levels.storyContext: A square window with a square cutout.

problems.statement: "A 10×10 square has a 3×3 square cut from one corner. What area remains?"

hints.text: Instead of adding pieces, here you SUBTRACT the missing piece from the whole.
Start with the full 10×10 square area, then subtract the cut-out.

problems.solutionExplanation: 91 square units. Full square: 10² = 100. Cut-out: 3² = 9. Remaining: 100 - 9 = 91.
problems.teachingPoint: Subtractive area: sometimes it is easier to compute the whole minus the missing piece than to add up all the remaining parts.

levels.name: Final Area Challenge
levels.storyContext: The final mountain challenge: a house-shaped figure.

problems.statement: "A house shape is made of a square (side 8) with a triangle (base 8, height 5) on top. What is the total area?"

hints.text: Break the house shape into two parts: the square body and the triangular roof.
Square area = 8 × 8. Triangle area = ½ × 8 × 5.
Square: 64. Triangle: ½ × 40 = 20. Total = 64 + 20 = ?

problems.solutionExplanation: 84 square units. Square body: 8² = 64. Triangular roof: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20. Total: 64 + 20 = 84.
problems.teachingPoint: Real-world shapes are often composites — houses, buildings, and land plots combine rectangles and triangles.

levels.name: Area Quick Compare
levels.storyContext: Which plot of land is bigger? Lizzie says you do not need to multiply...

problems.statement: "Without calculating, which has more area: a 7×9 rectangle or an 8×8 square?"

hints.text: Remember the optimization principle: for a fixed perimeter, which shape has the most area?
Both shapes have similar dimensions. The square is the "most balanced" rectangle.
Think about it this way: 7×9 = 63 and 8×8 = 64. The square wins — but can you see why WITHOUT multiplying?

problems.solutionExplanation: The 8×8 square has more area (64 vs 63). For shapes with similar total dimensions, the square always maximizes area.
problems.teachingPoint: Among rectangles with the same perimeter, the square always has the largest area — "spreading out" dimensions evenly is optimal.

signatureContent: Area units and why they are squared
